document_purpose: evidence-based clinical practice guidelines for diabetes care, updated annually, providing standardized recommendations for healthcare professionals
analyst_role: clinical guideline analyst or healthcare policy researcher

key_terminology.A1C: Glycated hemoglobin test measuring average blood glucose levels over 2-3 months
key_terminology.SGLT2: Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors, a class of diabetes medications
key_terminology.ADA Standards of Care: Annual comprehensive clinical practice guidelines for diabetes management

labeling_few_shots.text_snippet: Two of the main motivations for screening for diabetic retinopathy are to prevent loss of vision and to intervene with treatment when vision loss can be prevented or reversed.
labeling_few_shots.description: A clinical recommendation focused on the purpose and timing of screening for diabetic retinopathy in patients with diabetes.

labeling_few_shots.text_snippet: The Standards of Care includes discussion of evidence and clinical practice recommendations intended to optimize care for people with diabetes by assisting health care professionals and individuals in making shared decisions about diabetes care.
labeling_few_shots.description: A core methodology principle emphasizing collaborative decision-making between healthcare providers and patients regarding diabetes management strategies.

labeling_few_shots.text_snippet: A scientific review is a balanced systematic review and analysis of literature on a scientific or medical topic related to diabetes. A scientific review is not an ADA position and does not contain clinical practice recommendations but is produced under the auspices of the ADA by invited experts.
labeling_few_shots.description: A type of ADA publication that provides evidence-based analysis without direct clinical recommendations, serving as background for Standards of Care.

delta_change_types.name: Guideline Clarification
delta_change_types.description: when existing recommendations are restated with more precise language or additional context without changing the core recommendation

delta_change_types.name: New Recommendation Addition
delta_change_types.description: when a new clinical recommendation is introduced based on emerging evidence or clinical need

delta_change_types.name: Recommendation Strengthening
delta_change_types.description: when existing recommendations are reinforced with stronger evidence or expanded scope

delta_change_types.name: Recommendation Reversal
delta_change_types.description: when a previous recommendation is explicitly contradicted or reversed due to new evidence or safety concerns

delta_change_types.name: No Meaningful Change
delta_change_types.description: when two versions address the same topic but the differences are editorial or insignificant to clinical practice

fusion_change_types.name: Concordant with Guideline
fusion_change_types.description: the patient/case finding agrees with what the guideline recommends or expects

fusion_change_types.name: Deviates — Clinically Significant
fusion_change_types.description: the patient/case finding meaningfully conflicts with the guideline in a way that matters clinically

fusion_change_types.name: Deviates — Borderline
fusion_change_types.description: the patient/case finding is outside the guideline's expectation but only marginally/not clearly significant

fusion_change_types.name: Guideline Silent on This Case
fusion_change_types.description: the guideline reference doesn't actually address this specific finding/scenario

delta_field_meaning.requirements: clinical prerequisites or conditions that must be met before a recommendation can be applied, including patient characteristics, diagnostic criteria, or prior treatment steps
delta_field_meaning.deprecated_items: previously recommended treatments, screening methods, or clinical approaches that are no longer endorsed due to new evidence or safety concerns
delta_field_meaning.new_items: newly introduced recommendations, screening protocols, medications, or clinical strategies that represent updated best practices

delta_few_shots.topic: SGLT2 inhibitor use in heart failure
delta_few_shots.version_a: SGLT2 inhibitors were recommended primarily for glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease.
delta_few_shots.version_b: SGLT2 inhibitors are now recommended for patients with type 2 diabetes and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction regardless of glycemic control status.
delta_few_shots.analysis: The 2026 update expands the indication for SGLT2 inhibitors beyond glycemic management to include heart failure treatment, reflecting new cardiovascular outcome evidence. This represents a significant expansion of therapeutic use with implications for cardiology and endocrinology practice.

delta_few_shots.version_a: A1C targets for older adults with diabetes were generally set at <7.5% for healthy individuals and <8.5% for those with multiple comorbidities.
delta_few_shots.version_b: A1C targets for older adults are now individualized based on patient-specific factors including life expectancy, cognitive function, and hypoglycemia risk, with no fixed numeric targets recommended.
delta_few_shots.analysis: The 2026 update reverses the previous fixed A1C targets for older adults, replacing them with individualized goals based on comprehensive geriatric assessment. This represents a fundamental shift from population-based to patient-centered care in this vulnerable population.

qna_few_shots.q: Why did the ADA Standards of Care 2026 expand SGLT2 inhibitor recommendations beyond glycemic control?
qna_few_shots.a: The expansion reflects new cardiovascular outcome trial evidence demonstrating that SGLT2 inhibitors reduce heart failure hospitalization and cardiovascular mortality in patients with type 2 diabetes, independent of their glucose-lowering effects. This led to a broader indication for cardiovascular protection.

qna_few_shots.q: How should clinicians approach A1C targets in older adults according to the 2026 Standards of Care?
qna_few_shots.a: Clinicians should abandon fixed A1C targets for older adults and instead use individualized goals based on comprehensive geriatric assessment including life expectancy, cognitive status, functional independence, and hypoglycemia risk. The focus shifts from glycemic control to overall health and quality of life outcomes.

evolution_few_shot.topic: SGLT2 inhibitor use in heart failure
evolution_few_shot.foundation: SGLT2 inhibitors were initially recommended for glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease.
value_added: Expanded indication to include heart failure with reduced ejection fraction regardless of diabetes status
New evidence supporting cardiovascular mortality reduction
Inclusion in multiple cardiovascular guidelines beyond diabetes care
evolution_few_shot.narrative: The 2026 Standards of Care builds on the 2025 foundation by extending SGLT2 inhibitor recommendations to broader heart failure populations. This evolution reflects growing evidence that these medications provide cardiovascular benefits independent of their glucose-lowering effects, transforming them from diabetes-specific agents to cardiovascular therapeutics with ancillary glycemic benefits.
